title: Particles and States of Matter
seo_title: Year 7 Science: Particles and States of Matter Worksheets (Particle Model, Density)
standard_code: KS3 Chemistry: The particulate nature of matter
standard_text: The properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure; changes of state in terms of the particle model; the differences in arrangements, in motion and in closeness of particles explaining changes of state, shape and density; conservation of material and of mass, and reversibility, in melting, freezing, evaporation, sublimation, condensation, dissolving; Brownian motion in gases; diffusion in liquids and gases driven by differences in concentration.
meta_desc: Free Year 7 science worksheets on particles and states of matter: the particle model of solids, liquids and gases, changes of state, melting and boiling points, diffusion and density. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Particles explain solids, liquids and gases.
key_sub: Density = mass ÷ volume. Mass is conserved in a change of state.
body_html:
How to think about it

Everything is made of particles, and how they are arranged decides the state.

  • Solid: regular pattern, vibrate on the spot. Liquid: close together, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, move fast in all directions.
  • Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and sublimating are changes of state. Mass is conserved.
  • Density = mass ÷ volume. Particles diffuse from high to low concentration.
Example

Mass 60 g, volume 20 cm³. Density?

60 ÷ 20

Answer: 3 g/cm³

Example

Gas to liquid is called?

It happens on a cold window

Answer: condensing

Common mistakes

  • Thinking particles in a solid do not move.
  • Thinking particles get bigger when heated.
  • Thinking mass is lost when ice melts.

faq.q: How are particles arranged in solids, liquids and gases?
faq.a: In a solid they are close together in a regular pattern and vibrate. In a liquid they are close together but move past each other. In a gas they are far apart and move quickly.

faq.q: Is mass lost when ice melts?
faq.a: No. The same particles are still there, so the mass of the water equals the mass of the ice.
Density = mass ÷ volume. A block of 60 g with a volume of 20 cm³ has a density of 3 g/cm³.
